messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When the bomb went off in the financial district, Rithy was standing at his teller window, counting out a customer’s deposit. The blast threw him against the counter, and for a long moment the world was just noise and dust and the smell of burnt wiring. He helped a woman to the emergency exit, but in the chaos he also pushed past a man who had fallen, stepping over him without stopping. That moment—the feeling of his shoe landing beside the man’s hand, the decision not to pause—had lodged itself in Rithy’s chest like a splinter he could not remove. Six months later, he still woke at 3 a.m. with his heart hammering, convinced he heard footsteps in the hallway. He would lie still, listening, before getting up to check the locks on his apartment door, then the windows, then the locks again. What frightened him most was not the memory of the explosion itself, but the certainty that he was no longer the person he had been. He had always thought of himself as someone who would stop, who would help. The fact that he had not—that he had chosen his own survival over a stranger’s—meant, he believed, that he could not trust himself in any real crisis. This belief made the world feel dangerous in a new way: if he could not rely on his own instincts, then every crowded street, every sudden noise, every stranger who walked too close behind him became a potential threat. He began checking over his shoulder constantly, especially when leaving the bank at the end of his shift.

Rithy had come to believe that the only way to manage this fear was to stay busy. He volunteered for extra shifts, often arriving before the branch opened and leaving after the last customer had gone. The work was numbing and repetitive, and that was exactly what he needed: as long as he was counting cash or processing deposits, he did not have to think about what had happened, or about the person he had become. But the overwork came at a cost. He was too exhausted to see friends, and he had stopped dating entirely. His divorce, which had been finalized two years before the bombing, had left him wary of intimacy, and the attack had only deepened that wariness. Being close to someone meant being vulnerable, and vulnerability now felt intolerable. He could not imagine explaining to a partner why he woke up at night to check the locks, or why he sometimes flinched when a customer raised their voice. It was easier to be alone.

The suppression of his thoughts was a constant effort. When a memory surfaced—the sound of the blast, the taste of dust, the sight of the man on the ground—Rithy would immediately redirect his attention to something else: a transaction, a schedule, the pattern on the floor tiles. He had taught himself to do this so quickly that the memories often felt like they were barely there at all. But the effort of holding them at bay left him irritable. He snapped at a coworker who asked him a question during a busy lunch rush, and he had to apologize afterward. The irritability bothered him, because it felt like further evidence that he was not the person he used to be. He had always been patient, easygoing. Now he was someone who barked at colleagues and pushed past strangers.

The cycle tightened over the course of the year. The more he doubted himself, the more he scanned for danger. The more he scanned for danger, the more exhausted he became. The more exhausted he became, the less he trusted his own judgment, and the more he withdrew. By the time he finally called a therapist, he was working sixty-hour weeks, sleeping in fragments, and had not had a meaningful conversation with anyone in months. What brought him to the appointment was not the fear or the fatigue, but a moment of quiet: standing alone in the bank vault after closing, he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt anything other than vigilance. He was afraid that if he stopped checking, stopped working, stopped suppressing, something terrible would happen. But he was also afraid that nothing would happen at all—that he would simply go on like this, hollow and watchful, forever.
